analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to provide up to seven paid sick days for contagious illness.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2009 H1N1 flu pandemic, this bill would have required employers with 15 or more workers to give each full-time employee at least seven days of paid sick time each year (part-timers a pro-rated amount) to use when they or their children are sick with a contagious illness, when a health authority says their presence would endanger others, or when a workplace or child's school closes because of contagion. It would have protected workers from being fired or penalized for using the leave, let them sue to enforce it, credited employers who already offered equivalent paid leave, and expired after two years. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 50 to 60 million workers the bill's findings say had no paid sick leave — disproportionately low-wage workers, only 1 in 4 of whom had paid sick days, and often in jobs with frequent public contact — would gain guaranteed paid time to stay home when sick or caring for a sick child, without losing pay or their job [S3]. Employers who already provided equivalent paid leave would gain a level playing field, since competitors could no longer cut costs by denying leave [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Full-time employees at covered employers would get at least 7 days of paid sick time each year; part-time workers would get a pro rata share based on hours worked [S3].

The leave could be used when a worker or their child has symptoms of a contagious illness, needs diagnosis, care, or prevention, or when a health authority says the worker's presence would endanger others — precisely the situations, like H1N1 exposure, where a worker without leave is forced to choose between a paycheck and public health [S3].

It also covers closures: paid time if the workplace shuts down due to contagious illness or if a child's school or child care program closes, and it bars employers from making workers find their own replacements before taking leave [S3].

The bill includes anti-retaliation protections — employers may not fire, discriminate against, or count sick days against workers under attendance policies for using the leave — and gives workers a private right to sue, modeled on Family and Medical Leave Act remedies [S3].
Employers with existing paid-leave policies meeting the same standard are not required to add anything, and state or local laws with greater protections are left in place [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — businesses and government entities with 15 or more employees — would pay for up to seven paid sick days per full-time employee per year (pro-rated for part-timers), plus compliance costs for notices, recordkeeping, and adjusting attendance policies [S3]. The bill requires no payout of unused time at separation and exempts employers whose existing policies already meet the standard, which limits but does not eliminate the cost [S3].

drawbacks.text: Covered employers would bear the direct cost of up to seven paid days per employee per year, a burden that falls hardest on small and low-margin businesses just above the 15-employee threshold, and the bill's rapid effective date (15 to 30 days after enactment) would have given them little time to adjust [S3].

The bill was temporary by design — it would terminate two years after enactment — so workers and employers would face a new federal mandate on an expiring clock, creating uncertainty rather than a permanent standard [S3].

Enforcement relies partly on employee lawsuits and federal court actions modeled on the Family and Medical Leave Act, which can impose litigation costs on employers and does not guarantee quick relief for a worker denied leave [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real and time-sensitive: during the 2009 H1N1 emergency, millions of workers without paid sick leave faced a choice between following public-health guidance to stay home and keeping their pay or their jobs, and the bill's own findings cite CDC estimates that staying home could cut pandemic infections by 15 to 34 percent [S3]. The costs are also real: covered employers would fund the leave, a burden that falls hardest on low-margin businesses and firms just above the 15-employee threshold, and even supporters would acknowledge the 2-year sunset and rapid 15-to-30-day implementation timeline left little room to adjust payroll systems or plan for the expense. The bill softened the blow by crediting existing paid-leave policies and barring payout of unused time at separation, but the core tradeoff — worker security and slower disease spread versus a new employer mandate — remained. The bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, then to a subcommittee in January 2010, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 17, 2009, during the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, and referred the same day to the Education and Labor, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform committees [S5].

On January 4, 2010, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections of the Education and Labor Committee; the action history records no further activity — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The bill remained a one-chamber House bill with six cosponsors through the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011, and all pending legislation died at that point [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 15 or more employees — particularly retail, food service, and hospitality firms — avoided the cost of a new paid-sick-day mandate, and no federal paid sick leave requirement was created during the H1N1 pandemic.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; support was confined to the Democratic side — the sponsor and 6 of 253 House Democrats as cosponsors, with no Republican support recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more workers (retail, food service, hospitality, and other low-wage, public-facing sectors)
industries.note: These employers would fund up to seven paid sick days per employee per year, a cost concentrated in industries that employ the most workers without paid leave. Because low-wage workers are the most likely to have frequent public contact, the mandate targets exactly the businesses least likely to offer leave voluntarily.

The bill imposes compliance, recordkeeping, and litigation exposure (the civil-action provision mirrors the Family and Medical Leave Act) on covered employers, though it exempts those with already-compliant paid-leave policies and does not require payouts for unused time. National business groups opposed paid-sick-day mandates of this kind during this period.
